title: five who said yes
hook: the five people dressed alike at the front of the parade, and the day in 1699 they stand in for

segments.voice: Yesterday: the turban, a crown you tie yourself, and the steel kara. Today, the morning in 1699 that both trace back to.

At the front of a Sikh parade, ahead of the float carrying the scripture, walk five people dressed alike, swords held upright. They aren't security, and they aren't there for show. They're standing in for five people from more than three hundred years ago, who did something nobody in the crowd that day expected.
screen: `FIVE, DRESSED ALIKE, AT THE FRONT.` → `NOT SECURITY. NOT FOR SHOW.` → `STANDING IN FOR FIVE.`

segments.voice: Spring, 1699, at Anandpur in the hills of Punjab. A huge crowd has gathered for the harvest festival, Vaisakhi. The tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, walks out with a drawn sword and asks a question that silences everyone: who will give their head for the faith? One man stands, Daya Ram. The Guru takes him into a tent and comes back out alone. Then he asks again. Four more stand, one at a time. What happened inside that tent, the tellings differ. What they agree on is what came next: all five walked out alive, dressed alike, beside the Guru. They're remembered as the Panj Pyare: panj, five, pyare, beloved. And look who they were. A shopkeeper from Lahore. A farmer from near Delhi. A water-carrier from Puri, on the eastern coast. A cloth printer from Dwarka, in the far west. A barber from Bidar, in the south. Castes that, around them, would never have shared a meal, from homes a thousand miles apart. They became the first of the Khalsa, the community of committed Sikhs: one family. The men took one name, Singh, lion, and Sikh women carry the name Kaur. Two names that rank no one.
screen: `WHO WILL GIVE THEIR HEAD?` · `ALL FIVE WALK OUT ALIVE.` · `FIVE CASTES, FIVE CORNERS OF INDIA.` · `SINGH AND KAUR — ONE FAMILY.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, picture the crowd on the hillside, gone quiet. On the second, picture one person standing up when nobody else will. On the third, sit a little taller yourself, the way someone does when they stand for what they love.
Panj Pyare. The five beloved: strangers from across India who stood up, and walked out one family. Fourth word.
Your line: five strangers, one family. The five at the front of every parade are standing in for them. That's day four.

howItsDone: At every amrit initiation, five initiated Sikhs stand in as the Panj Pyare, and five Sikhs dressed alike lead Nagar Kirtan processions ahead of the Guru Granth Sahib; the Khalsa's founding is celebrated every year at Vaisakhi.

what a scholar hears: the Vaisakhi of 1699 at Anandpur. the five took the name Singh, and their first names, Daya, Dharam, Himmat, Mohkam and Sahib, mean compassion, righteousness, courage, steadfastness and sovereignty.

story.title: the Guru who knelt
story.text: The five have just been initiated, sipping water sweetened with sugar and stirred with a double-edged sword. Then the Guru does something nobody expects. He kneels in front of the five he has just made, and asks them to initiate him, the same way. The teacher becomes the student of his own students. A later poet put the moment into one line Sikhs still sing: wonderful is the Guru who is also the disciple.
story.source: Sikh tradition of the Vaisakhi of 1699; the line 'aape gur chela' from a var attributed to Bhai Gurdas II

notes: New lesson, written 2026-10-06 from the audience research (proposed first week, day 4; top-20 moments 9 and 18).

The 1699 story is told in full on days 84–87 ('the call', 'the five beloved', 'sugar in the iron bowl', 'the Guru becomes the disciple'), and day 85's word is also Panj Pyare. Day 4 tells it briefly; a Keeper may want day 85's word changed later so the strand doesn't repeat.

The tent: the script says 'the tellings differ' and does not describe blood or killing (some tellings say goats were sacrificed; others hold the five were tested in other ways). Confirm this is gentle enough for day 4 (owner: don't freak people out early).

The five's origins and trades follow the common telling (day 85 uses the same list): Daya Ram, a khatri shopkeeper of Lahore; Dharam Das, a Jat farmer from near Delhi; Himmat Rai, a water-carrier from Puri; Mohkam Chand, a washerman or cloth printer from Dwarka; Sahib Chand, a barber from Bidar. Confirm.

Kaur: the script says only that 'Sikh women carry the name Kaur'; historians discuss when Kaur became universal for Sikh women, so the script doesn't say it was given in 1699. Confirm. 'Two names that rank no one' reflects the Singh/Kaur ideal; many Sikhs also keep family surnames.

Story: the Guru receiving amrit from the five; 'wah wah Gobind Singh aape gur chela' is attributed to Bhai Gurdas II (not the Bhai Gurdas of the Adi Granth). Sugar added to the water is told on day 86 (tradition credits the Guru's wife; versions differ on her name), so the story mentions sugar without naming her. Confirm.
